claims.text: Spin-polarized DFT can be used to determine whether a ferromagnetic ground state is present.
Spin-polarized DFT explicitly accounts for exchange interactions and spin-polarization effects.
Comparing the total energies of different magnetic configurations can identify the magnetic ground state.
The proposed initial material is a high-entropy or disordered metallic alloy related to Al0.1CrCoFeNi.
Ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and non-magnetic configurations should be compared under identical relaxed structural conditions.
The calculations should be performed at zero temperature using an exchange-correlation treatment such as GGA or GGA+U.
Simulation cells must be sufficiently large to capture relevant clustering or ordering effects.
Local atomic ordering and clustering can affect the distribution of exchange interactions in these alloys.
Including spin degrees of freedom in DFT permits evaluation of exchange splitting in the electronic structure.
If a ferromagnetic configuration has lower total energy than competing configurations, the ground state is ferromagnetic.
Exchange-correlation interactions can stabilize ferromagnetic order.
An energetically favored ferromagnetic state will exhibit lower calculated total energy than non-magnetic or antiferromagnetic configurations.
An energetically favored ferromagnetic state will exhibit a net magnetic moment.
Non-spin-polarized DFT does not distinguish among magnetic orderings.
Predictions may depend on the exchange-correlation functional, simulation-cell size, and treatment of local chemical order.
Zero-temperature DFT calculations may not capture temperature-dependent magnetic effects.
Calculated energy differences and magnetic moments can vary with methodological details.
Complex atomic clustering in high-entropy alloys introduces additional uncertainty into magnetic predictions.

contradictions.description: The core hypothesis says the method can determine whether a ferromagnetic ground state is present, but the falsification rule treats a DFT prediction of a non-ferromagnetic state accompanied by an experimental absence of ferromagnetism as falsification. Such agreement would instead support the method's ability to identify the absence of a ferromagnetic ground state.
